All studies included in the analysis were conducted in adult populations to evaluate the effects of lower TFA intake compared to higher intake on pre-specified priority health outcomes. 5. The studies were primarily conducted in North America, Europe, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Asia. 6. The absolute effect (per 1,000 people) is calculated using the formula: absolute effect = 1,000 × [event rate × (1 – relative risk, RR)]. The magnitude of the absolute effect in real-world settings depends on baseline risk, which can vary across populations. 8. All outcomes in this evidence profile are considered critical for decision-making. Outcomes are categorized as not important, important, or critical during the guideline development process. Only critical outcomes are used to determine the overall certainty of the evidence supporting a recommendation. 9. Both cohorts included in the analysis for this outcome consisted of similar populations of health professionals, and the same or very similar dietary assessment tools were used. 10. Due to concerns about potential bias from the use of similar assessment tools and indirectness resulting from specific study populations, the outcome was conservatively downgraded once for risk of bias and indirectness. 11. Heterogeneity was significant, with an I² value greater than 50%. This led to a single downgrade. 12. The number of comparisons is provided in parentheses. 13. All studies included in this analysis were strictly controlled, relatively short-term dietary trials. 14. Studies with crossover and Latin-square designs were considered to have a low risk of bias for randomization, even if randomization was not explicitly stated, as all participants were intended to receive all treatments. This minimizes the likelihood of baseline differences having a systematic effect on study results. 15. Two studies with parallel designs were assessed as having an unclear risk of bias regarding randomization because it was not specified whether participants were randomized. 16. Blinding was not considered a significant source of bias because all interventions involved food provision. Even if participants could distinguish between intervention and control diets, this was not expected to affect compliance due to the study design and conduct. 17. Bias from unblinded outcome assessment was considered very low. There was no indication of widespread attrition bias, selective reporting, or other significant sources of bias. 18. Qualitative assessment of the included studies showed that point estimates across individual studies were similar, and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) overlapped, suggesting that inconsistency was not serious. 19. Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is an indirect measure of patient-important CVD outcomes. However, LDL cholesterol is a well-established biomarker for assessing the effects of interventions on CVD risk and is considered by many to be a causal factor for atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease. Therefore, it was not downgraded for indirectness. 20. Imprecision was assessed using the 95% CI of the regression coefficient as a proxy for the 95% CI of a pooled estimate of effect. The regression coefficient provides an estimate of the effect of reducing TFA intake on LDL cholesterol, and the 95% CI measures the variability of that effect. The 95% CI does not cross a threshold of important benefit or harm. 21. Visual inspection of the funnel plot did not suggest publication bias. 22. The relative effect is represented by a regression coefficient, interpreted as the change in LDL cholesterol when 1% of total energy intake from TFAs is replaced with an isocaloric amount of polyunsaturated fatty acids. 23.
